opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, that's a really interesting piece of history. Back around 2016 and 2017, OpenAI had a project, World of Bits and the Universe platform, where the idea was: let's give an RL agent a browser, have it look at pixels, move the mouse, click and type, and see if it can learn to do useful things on the web. And honestly, it didn't really work. The agents could handle some very simple MiniWoB-style tasks, like clicking a button or picking an item from a little form, but nothing close to a general web agent.

The way I understand it, the problem wasn't really the RL algorithms. The problem was that the agent started from nothing. It had no idea what a button was, what text meant, or why you'd want to book a flight. You're asking reinforcement learning to discover language, visual understanding, common sense and the task logic all at once, from an extremely sparse reward signal. The exploration space is enormous. Random clicking almost never stumbles onto success, so there's almost nothing to learn from. It's like asking a baby to learn to use a computer purely by trial and error, with a cookie every few thousand random clicks.

What changed later is the prior. Once you have large pretrained language models, and then multimodal models, the agent already understands the web page, already knows roughly what "submit" or "search" means, and can reason about what to do next. RL then isn't learning everything from scratch. It's refining and aligning behavior that's already mostly reasonable. That's a completely different regime. Exploration becomes meaningful because the policy proposes sensible actions, and the reward signal actually has something to shape.

So I'd say the lesson isn't "RL for agents doesn't work." It's that RL is a powerful amplifier, but it needs a good foundation to amplify. The early attempt was in some sense the right vision but the wrong time. The pieces needed, a strong pretrained model as the starting point, good infrastructure, and reasonable reward design, just weren't there yet. Today a lot of what we do with agentic RL is the same dream, finally standing on the shoulders of pretraining.

fable-5.1.text:
You're asking about World of Bits. That was around 2016, 2017, when I was still at OpenAI. The idea was very ambitious: we wanted an agent that could operate a browser the way a human does, click buttons, fill forms, book flights, basically do anything on the internet. If you could solve that, you'd have a general agent, because the web is a universal interface.

The result, honestly, was that it didn't work, and I think the reason it didn't work is more interesting than the failure itself. Pure reinforcement learning from pixels and raw actions is just incredibly sample-inefficient. The action space is enormous, every pixel coordinate is a possible click, and the reward is extremely sparse. You only get a signal when you complete the whole task. So the agent spends almost all its time clicking randomly and learning nothing. We tried demonstrations, we tried curriculum, and we could get it to do small toy tasks, but it never generalized to real websites.

Looking back, the deeper problem was that the agent had no prior knowledge. It didn't know what a button was, what "submit" meant, what a date looked like. A human child using a browser for the first time already has years of world knowledge. We were asking RL to learn language, vision, and common sense all from scratch, through a reward signal of zero or one. That's basically impossible.

So the lesson I took away is that RL is a very good optimizer but a very poor learner of knowledge. You need the knowledge to come from somewhere else. And this is exactly what changed with large language models. Today, when people build web agents on top of GPT-4 or Claude, the model already understands what a webpage is, it can read the text, it knows what the user wants. RL becomes a fine-tuning step on top of a strong prior, not the whole story. In that sense, World of Bits wasn't wrong about the goal. It was just about eight years too early, because the foundation wasn't there yet.

astra-6.text:
I’d interpret it as an idea that was ahead of the capabilities available at the time. Clicking around a web page sounds simple, but the agent has to understand what it’s looking at, figure out which actions matter, and connect a long sequence of actions to a reward that may arrive only at the end. If you’re trying to learn all of that through reinforcement learning from scratch, exploration becomes extremely difficult.

So I wouldn’t take a disappointing outcome as evidence that reinforcement learning can’t work for web agents. It suggests that reinforcement learning alone wasn’t enough to give the agent a useful starting point. A model that already understands language and has some knowledge of how interfaces work faces a much more manageable learning problem: improving how it acts, rather than discovering everything from zero.

sol-6.1.text:
My understanding is that the attempt ran into a fundamental difficulty: a web page gives an agent a huge number of possible actions, but very little feedback about which actions are useful. If the agent has to learn everything through trial and error, even a seemingly simple task can require an enormous amount of exploration.

So I wouldn’t interpret the outcome as showing that reinforcement learning cannot work for web agents. It showed how difficult it is to start from scratch. An agent needs some prior understanding of language, interfaces, and what people are trying to accomplish. With that foundation, reinforcement learning can refine its behavior instead of having to discover everything through random clicking.
